title: "Implementing Iterator from Scratch"

# Implementing Iterator from Scratch

Implement `Iterator` when the sequence is not a slice and not a combination of standard adaptors. You write `next`. Consumers you did not write (`collect`, `for`, `nth`) start working.

## The concept

```rust
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> { /* you write this */ }
}
```

Store the cursor in the iterator, not in a global. Return `None` when the sequence is finished, and keep returning `None` after that if you want `FusedIterator` (a later recipe). A borrowing iterator holds a reference and a lifetime. An owning iterator holds the data.

## Recipe 35 — Iterating over fields of a struct

Three named fields are not a slice. A tiny index still makes them one sequence.

```rust
struct Sample {
    temp: i32,
    fan: i32,
    volts: i32,
}

struct SampleIter<'a> {
    sample: &'a Sample,
    index: u8,
}

impl<'a> Iterator for SampleIter<'a> {
    type Item = &'a i32;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        let value = match self.index {
            0 => &self.sample.temp,
            1 => &self.sample.fan,
            2 => &self.sample.volts,
            _ => return None,
        };
        self.index += 1;
        Some(value)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let sample = Sample { temp: 20, fan: 1200, volts: 12 };
    let values: Vec<i32> = SampleIter { sample: &sample, index: 0 }.copied().collect();
    assert_eq!(values, [20, 1200, 12]);
}
```

The `match` is tedious on purpose. If the fields are a real list, store a `[i32; 3]` or a `Vec` and iterate that. Use this pattern when the fields have different names and a fixed order that callers rely on.

## Recipe 36 — An iterator with internal state

Fibonacci needs two numbers of memory. They live on the iterator.

```rust
struct Fib {
    curr: u64,
    next: u64,
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        let out = self.curr;
        let sum = self.curr.saturating_add(self.next);
        self.curr = self.next;
        self.next = sum;
        Some(out)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let first_eight: Vec<_> = Fib { curr: 0, next: 1 }.take(8).collect();
    assert_eq!(first_eight, [0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13]);
}
```

This iterator is infinite. `saturating_add` keeps the example from panicking if someone takes a huge prefix. A fallible sequence returns `None` at the end instead of `Some` forever.

## Recipe 37 — A borrowing iterator with a lifetime

The iterator must not outlive the slice it reads. The lifetime on the struct is that promise.

```rust
struct Windows<'a, T> {
    slice: &'a [T],
    start: usize,
    width: usize,
}

impl<'a, T> Iterator for Windows<'a, T> {
    type Item = &'a [T];

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        let end = self.start + self.width;
        if end > self.slice.len() {
            return None;
        }
        let window = &self.slice[self.start..end];
        self.start += 1;
        Some(window)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let readings = [10, 20, 30, 40];
    let windows: Vec<&[i32]> = Windows { slice: &readings, start: 0, width: 2 }.collect();
    assert_eq!(windows, [&[10, 20][..], &[20, 30][..], &[30, 40][..]]);
}
```

`Item = &'a [T]` can be returned even though `next` only has `&mut self`, because the slice data lives in `readings`, not in the iterator. The standard library already has `slice::windows`. This recipe is the shape, not a replacement.

## Recipe 38 — Iterating over a recursive data structure

A tree walk can use an explicit stack. That keeps `next` iterative and avoids a recursive call per node.

```rust
struct Node {
    value: i32,
    children: Vec<Node>,
}

struct Walk<'a> {
    stack: Vec<&'a Node>,
}

impl<'a> Iterator for Walk<'a> {
    type Item = i32;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        let node = self.stack.pop()?;
        for child in node.children.iter().rev() {
            self.stack.push(child);
        }
        Some(node.value)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let tree = Node {
        value: 1,
        children: vec![
            Node { value: 2, children: vec![Node { value: 4, children: vec![] }] },
            Node { value: 3, children: vec![] },
        ],
    };
    let order: Vec<_> = Walk { stack: vec![&tree] }.collect();
    assert_eq!(order, [1, 2, 4, 3]);
}
```

Children are pushed in reverse so the left child is popped first. The result is a pre-order walk. An in-order walk of a binary tree needs a different stack state. Do not recurse inside `next` along a spine that can be thousands of nodes deep. The call stack is smaller than you think.

## Recipe 39 — Implementing size_hint() for better collect() performance

`size_hint` returns `(lower, upper)`. `collect` uses the lower bound to allocate once when it can. A correct hint is an optimization. A hint that claims more items than you yield is still safe. A hint used by unsafe code that trusts the upper bound exactly is a different contract: `ExactSizeIterator::len` is that stricter promise.

```rust
struct Countdown {
    left: u32,
}

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        if self.left == 0 {
            return None;
        }
        self.left -= 1;
        Some(self.left)
    }

    fn size_hint(&self) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
        let n = self.left as usize;
        (n, Some(n))
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut ticks = Countdown { left: 3 };
    assert_eq!(ticks.size_hint(), (3, Some(3)));
    assert_eq!(ticks.next(), Some(2));
    assert_eq!(ticks.size_hint(), (2, Some(2)));

    let all: Vec<_> = Countdown { left: 4 }.collect();
    assert_eq!(all, [3, 2, 1, 0]);
}
```

Returning `(0, None)` from `size_hint` is always allowed and means "I will not help you allocate". `collect` then grows the `Vec` as items arrive. For a countdown you know the length, so say so. The upper bound must be honest if you set it: do not return `Some(n)` if you might yield more than `n`.
